headline: Bird flu took 11 million layers out while broilers barely moved
body: The companion to the broiler figure, and the two together are the whole story. US layers averaged 365 million in 2025, down 3% from 376 million, and eggs per layer slipped from 290 to 288 - which compounds into a 4% production drop, from 109 to 105 billion eggs. Broilers over the same period lost roughly 0.05% of throughput. Same virus, same country, same species of bird: one flock devastated, the other essentially untouched, because a broiler lives 47 days and a layer lives years.
source: Chickens and Eggs 2025 Summary

headline: Bird flu barely touches chicken wings
body: 168.62 million birds have been lost to avian influenza since 2022, and the headlines are relentless - but roughly 75% of those were egg-laying hens and 11% turkeys. Broilers were about 8%, which works out near 0.05% of the 9.58 billion broilers slaughtered each year. Broilers live only 47 days, sit on smaller farms, and get restocked fast, so their cumulative exposure is low. Bird flu moves the price of eggs. It does not meaningfully move the price or supply of wings.
source: The Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) Outbreak in Poultry, 2022-Present

headline: A dozen boneless wings takes about a third of a chicken
body: A 6.62 lb broiler carries roughly 691 g of boneless breast, and a commercial boneless wing is about 20 g of raw breast meat - so one bird makes around 34 of them. Twelve pieces is therefore about 0.35 of a chicken. A dozen bone-in wings needs six whole chickens. Same menu section, same price bracket, and roughly a seventeenfold difference in how many birds it took.
source: Fully Cooked Breaded Whole Muscle Boneless Chicken Wings, product specs

headline: A boneless wing contains no wing meat
body: It is breast meat, cut into chunks and breaded. Tyson's own foodservice catalogue files the product under "boneless wings & chunks" and describes it as whole muscle chicken breast - the industry is not hiding this, the name just does not mean what it says. The honest count of wings in a dozen boneless wings is zero.
source: Fully Cooked Breaded Whole Muscle Boneless Chicken Wings, product specs

headline: Breading a wing lowers its calories per gram
body: A breaded fried wing measures about 180 kcal per 100 g against 191 for raw - which reads backwards until you notice why. Breading adds carbohydrate and absorbed water, so the piece gets heavier faster than it gets more caloric. The wing on your plate has more total calories; it is simply less calorie-dense per gram. Chicken itself contains no carbohydrate at all, so every gram of carb in a fried wing is breading.
source: Fast foods, fried chicken, wing, meat and skin and breading (FDC 170360)

headline: 90% of bruising happens in the last 12 to 24 hours
body: Not during the seven weeks of grow-out - during catching, loading, transport, and shackling. By body region, bruises land on the breast 42% of the time, wings 33%, legs 25%. Almost all the damage in a 47-day life happens on the final day.
source: The Influence of Welfare Training on Bird Welfare and Carcass Quality in Two Commercial Poultry Primary Processing Plants

headline: How a plant chills its birds swings wing weight by 10%
body: Air chilling makes a carcass LOSE about 2.5-2.8% of its weight. Immersion chilling makes it GAIN 4% and sometimes over 9%. That gap is larger than any loss in this entire model - and it cannot change the answer by a fraction, because chilling changes what a wing weighs, not how many wings a chicken has. Buy wings by the pound and it matters enormously. Order a dozen and it does not matter at all.
source: Moisture retention by water- and air-chilled broilers, and effect of immersion or dry air chilling on carcass moisture retention

headline: A dozen eggs might have come from a single chicken
body: Wings and eggs ask the same question and get opposite answers. Twelve wings can never come from fewer than six chickens, because a chicken only has two. But a hen lays again tomorrow - so one hen, given about fifteen days, can fill an entire carton by herself. For eggs the honest answer runs from 1 chicken to 12, and which end you land on is a question about patience rather than biology.
source: Chickens and Eggs 2025 Summary

headline: With eggs, the floor rises to meet the ceiling
body: For wings the minimum is six and mixing through the supply chain pushes the real answer up toward twelve. For a same-day dozen of eggs the minimum is already twelve, so the floor and the ceiling meet and there is nothing left for the supply chain to move. Same question, opposite structure.
source: Chickens and Eggs 2025 Summary

headline: The farmer got about twelve cents for your dozen wings
body: Contract growers are paid 3.8 to 4.6 cents per pound of live weight. Six birds at 6.62 lb is 39.7 lb, so raising them earned the grower roughly $1.67 - and charging only the wings' share of that bird, about 12 cents. Growers are paid on a relative "tournament" basis against other farms delivering the same week, so two people doing identical work can be paid differently.
source: Fees paid to growers for raising broiler chickens varied widely in 2020

headline: Size grading deliberately separates a bird's two wings
body: Wings are weighed individually and sorted into jumbo, large, and medium. Two wings off the same bird rarely weigh exactly the same, so whenever they straddle a grade boundary they are routed into different boxes. The supply chain is not merely shuffling wings - at this step it is actively pulling pairs apart.
source: Mixing pool sizes reasoned from process equipment scale

headline: Alabama's hens lay 100 fewer eggs a year than Montana's
body: Alabama averaged 224 eggs per layer in 2025 and Montana 327. That is not worse farming - it is a different bird doing a different job. Alabama's layers are largely broiler-breeder hens producing hatching eggs that become meat chickens, and breeder hens lay far fewer eggs than table-egg strains. Of 377 million US layers, 60.7 million are hatching birds. A state's eggs-per-layer figure is mostly a readout of which mix it runs.
source: Chickens and Eggs 2025 Summary

headline: A restaurant "dozen wings" usually is not twelve wings
body: It is normally twelve PIECES - drumettes and flats. Each whole wing splits into a drumette, a flat, and a tip, and the tip is diverted to stock or rendering. So twelve pieces is six whole wings, which is three chickens' worth of anatomy. This single ambiguity changes the answer more than every processing loss combined.
source: A method of production of boneless chicken wings (drumettes and winglets) by separation of periosteum from bone without cutting skin and muscles

headline: 96% of chicken breasts now show white striping
body: White striping appears in essentially every commercial fillet. Severe woody breast runs about 12%, up from roughly 5% in 2012, and spaghetti meat 36%. More than 85% of fillets show more than one of these at once. Crucially the risk rises with live weight - so the big-bird deboning flocks that boneless product comes from are the worst affected. The real wing has no equivalent problem: wings are small working muscles and simply do not develop these myopathies.
source: Prevalence of breast muscle myopathies (spaghetti meat, woody breast, white striping) and associated risk factors in broiler chickens

headline: An Ohio chicken weighs half what a North Carolina chicken does
body: Ohio averaged 4.6 lb live weight in 2025; North Carolina averaged 8.4 lb. Same country, same year, same species - but they are different businesses. Ohio runs small birds for fast food and tray pack; North Carolina runs big birds for deboning. A pound of wings from each state represents a very different number of chickens.
source: Poultry Slaughter 2025 Summary

headline: A dozen eggs gathered in one day came from twelve different hens
body: A hen's ovulation cycle runs a little over 24 hours, so she lays at most about one egg a day. No hen laid two of the eggs in a same-day carton, which means twelve eggs means twelve hens - necessarily, with no estimating involved. It is the same kind of hard fact as a chicken having two wings, just arrived at through a clock instead of anatomy.
source: Chickens and Eggs 2025 Summary

headline: Wing tips and chicken paws are a $648 million export market
body: What Americans discard, China buys. Wing tips and paws are sold there for soups, stews, and snacking, and together they make up roughly a $648 million annual US export market. Paws fetch $0.80 to $1.00 a pound exported against $0.05 to $0.10 a pound as domestic animal feed - close to ten times the value for the identical product.
source: Chinese appetite for chicken paws proves a boon for U.S. producers

headline: Bird flu has cost 168 million birds since 2022
body: APHIS has confirmed highly pathogenic avian influenza in 1,689 commercial and backyard flocks between 2022 and April 2025, affecting 168.62 million birds. Almost all of that is layers and turkeys rather than broilers - a broiler reaches market in 47 days, which is a small window to be caught in, while a laying hen sits in one barn for well over a year. It is the main reason egg prices move and chicken wing prices mostly do not.
source: Confirmations of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza in Commercial and Backyard Flocks
publisher: USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service

headline: How many boneless wings a chicken makes is a business decision
body: A chicken has exactly two wings and no processor can change that. But the number of boneless wings per bird depends purely on how large the chunks are cut - somewhere between 25 and 43 pieces per bird for plausible portion sizes. For bone-in wings the floor is anatomy. For boneless it is a portioning choice, which is why this project stores the two with different confidence.
source: Fully Cooked Breaded Whole Muscle Boneless Chicken Wings, product specs

headline: Cage-free changes the hen's life, not the arithmetic
body: Cage-free, free range, and pasture-raised describe how hens are housed, not how many. A cage-free house still holds tens or hundreds of thousands of birds, so a same-day dozen is still twelve different hens. The only setting where the number genuinely falls is a backyard flock - six hens filling a carton over two weeks really is about six hens.
source: Chickens and Eggs, monthly releases 2026

headline: Chicken's footprint per bird has fallen every year
body: Between 2010 and 2020 the industry cut greenhouse gas per kg of live weight by 18%, fossil resource use by 22%, and land and water use by 13% each. Most of that came from feed efficiency: production rose 21% while feed consumption rose only 11%. The same efficiency drive that makes birds heavier and cheaper also made them lighter on the planet per pound.
source: Broiler Production System Life Cycle Assessment: 2020 Update
publisher: National Chicken Council / University of Arkansas

headline: The "chunks" are not wing either
body: Tyson files boneless wings under "boneless wings & chunks", which invites the question of whether chunks are a different cut. They are not. The ingredient statement reads "boneless, skinless chicken breast chunks with rib meat" - and rib meat is the portion left attached to the breast when it is deboned, part of the front quarter. It is not wing. Neither product contains any wing meat at all.
source: Boneless wings and chunks product line, ingredient statements

headline: FSIS condemns less than half a percent
body: Post-mortem condemnation ran 0.45% in 2025 and 0.46% in 2024 - remarkably stable. People expect this to be the big loss in the system. It is one of the smallest.
source: Poultry Slaughter 2025 Summary

headline: A cracked egg is not thrown away, it is rerouted
body: A cracked shell is a "check", and along with dirty eggs it counts as "restricted" - barred from the carton but allowed to go to a breaker plant to become liquid egg. So it leaves the shell-egg stream without leaving the food supply. USDA tolerances permit up to 7% checks in a Grade A pack at origin, though that is a ceiling a pack must stay under, not a rate anyone aims for.
source: United States Standards, Grades, and Weight Classes for Shell Eggs

headline: An egg carries more cholesterol than anything else here
body: 372 mg per 100 g, or about 186 mg in one large egg - the highest figure anywhere in this dataset by a wide margin. It is also the number whose dietary meaning changed most in living memory: the 2015 Dietary Guidelines dropped the explicit 300 mg-a-day cap that had stood for decades. Worth knowing what an egg contains. What that means for your diet is a clinical question, and this project has no standing to answer it.
source: Egg, whole, raw, fresh (FDC 171287)

headline: Grading splits a chicken's wings apart, but cannot split her eggs
body:
This is a modelling choice worth stating plainly rather than burying. Wings and eggs are both weighed and sorted, but the step does different work. A bird has exactly two wings, so weighing them routes a pair into different boxes whenever they straddle a grade boundary - the supply chain actively pulls the pair apart. An egg arrives at the grader already alone, because a hen laid one that day and nothing pairs it with another. There is no pair for grading to break.
So we model egg grading as ordinary mixing and wing grading as active separation. It is a judgement about mechanism, not a figure from a source, and it is the kind of assumption that should be visible.
source: United States Standards, Grades, and Weight Classes for Shell Eggs

headline: A dozen wings represents about five pounds of feed
body: At a feed conversion of 1.69 and a 6.57 lb market weight, one broiler eats about 11 lb of feed. The six birds behind a dozen wings ate roughly 67 lb between them - but the wings are only about 7% of the bird, so their honest share is close to 4.9 lb of corn and soy. The rest of that feed became somebody else's breast fillet.
source: U.S. Broiler Performance

headline: The flat has a better meat yield than the drumette
body: The drumette is heavier - 39.9 g against 30.7 g bone-in - but the flat yields 80.1% boneless meat against the drumette's 74.9%. Bigger does not mean meatier.
source: A method of production of boneless chicken wings (drumettes and winglets) by separation of periosteum from bone without cutting skin and muscles

headline: A dozen wings is not six chickens' worth of carbon
body: One broiler carries about 2.90 kg of CO2 equivalent across its whole life. It is tempting to multiply that by six - but wings are only about 7% of the bird, and the breast, thighs and drums went to other plates. Allocated by mass, a dozen wings carries closer to 1.3 kg CO2 equivalent. Charging the whole bird to the wings would overstate it roughly fourteenfold.
source: Broiler Production System Life Cycle Assessment: 2020 Update
publisher: National Chicken Council / University of Arkansas

headline: Some plants run 175 birds a minute, others 140
body: Plants under the New Poultry Inspection System may run 175 birds per minute; everyone else is capped at 140. That matters for wings specifically, because the damage that breaks them happens at shackling, and comment records tie faster lines to birds being hung improperly. Regulators counter that fast plants meet food safety standards - which is true, and a different question. Salmonella performance tells you nothing about how many wings got broken.
source: Maximum Line Speed Rates for Young Chicken and Turkey Establishments Operating Under the New Poultry Inspection System
publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service / Federal Register

headline: Broiler mortality has been getting worse since 2013
body: It hit a historic low of 3.7% in 2013 and has climbed to 5.93% by 2024, even as feed conversion kept improving from 1.75 to 1.69. Birds are more efficient than they have ever been and also dying more often.
source: U.S. Broiler Performance

headline: Getting a dozen eggs in one day actually takes about fifteen hens
body: Twelve hens is the floor, but hens do not lay every single day. At the US average rate of 0.789 eggs per hen per day, you need roughly 15.2 hens on hand to collect twelve eggs before sundown. The floor is what is physically possible; fifteen is what it actually takes.
source: Chickens and Eggs 2025 Summary

headline: Every wing has a third segment you never see
body: A whole wing is a drumette, a flat, and a tip. The tip is mostly skin, bone, and cartilage with almost no meat, so it is cut off and diverted before the wings ever reach a restaurant. When a menu says twelve wings, twelve tips went somewhere else.
source: A method of production of boneless chicken wings (drumettes and winglets) by separation of periosteum from bone without cutting skin and muscles

headline: At home, wing tips become stock, pet food, or fertilizer
body: Tips that do not get exported are ground into pet food, rendered into chemicals and fertilizer, or simmered into commercial stock. Rendering the whole volume would return less than a tenth of what the export market pays, which is why a trade dispute over chicken feet is a real and expensive thing.
source: Chinese appetite for chicken paws proves a boon for U.S. producers

headline: "Wings" is a regulated word, and boneless wings comply with it
body: USDA standards say a product labelled wings must be the entire wing, all muscle and skin intact, with only the tip removable - and that where bone has been removed the name must say so. "Boneless wing" satisfies that rule by disclosing the missing bone. The label is not a loophole; it is doing exactly what the regulation asks, which is why the name survives despite containing no wing.
source: Food Standards and Labeling Policy Book
publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service

headline: Wings are the most damaged part of the chicken, by far
body: Median wing injuries run 5.7% per load. Legs, breast, and shoulders are each under 1%. Wings stick out, they get caught, and they break during catching, loading, and shackling. This is the single largest loss in the model and the main reason it takes more than six chickens.
source: Rearing and handling injuries in broiler chickens and risk factors for wing injuries during loading

headline: An egg carries wing-like protein with a third less fat
body: Per 100 g an egg has 12.56 g of protein against a raw wing's 17.5 g, but only 9.51 g of fat against 12.8 g. The wing loses on that trade because of what it is: mostly skin, bone and small muscles, so its skin-to-meat ratio is high before anyone has breaded or fried it.
source: Egg, whole, raw, fresh (FDC 171287)

headline: Cooking changes the weight, never the count
body: Frying costs a wing roughly 20% of its mass, which matters a great deal for food cost and not at all here. Twelve wings go into the fryer, twelve wings come out. Cook loss has zero effect on how many chickens it took.
source: Placeholder pending research

headline: About three quarters of a live chicken becomes sellable meat
body: 63.44 billion lb went in live; 48.01 billion lb came out ready-to-cook. That is a dressing yield of 75.67% - and it is not an estimate. It falls straight out of two totals USDA measures directly.
source: National dressing yield derived from NASS totals

headline: The egg numbers check out against themselves, twice
body: Average layers times eggs per layer reproduces reported total production for every one of the 31 states with 2025 figures. And 288 eggs a year divided by 365 days gives 0.789 eggs per hen per day, matching the 78.7 to 79.9 eggs per 100 layers that USDA reports from an entirely separate monthly survey. Two unrelated tables landing on the same answer is the strongest validation anywhere in this project.
source: Chickens and Eggs 2025 Summary

headline: Restaurant kitchens waste 4-13% of what they buy
body: EPA figures put food waste at 4% to 13% of food costs in commercial kitchens, with spoilage alone running 1-5% in prepare-ahead operations and 1-6% in cook-to-order. That independently brackets the ~4.2% of purchases the foodservice data says goes unused - two different bodies measuring different things and landing in the same place. It is why restaurant loss is one of the better-evidenced numbers in this model despite sounding like the softest.
source: Food waste reduction in commercial kitchens (Winnow, EPA materials)

headline: The US produced 19.16 billion whole wings in 2025
body: 9,579,797,000 broilers were slaughtered, and each had two wings. That is about 56 whole wings for every person in the country, every year.
source: Poultry Slaughter 2025 Summary

headline: Four companies produce well over half the chicken in America
body: Tyson at 21.3%, Pilgrim's Pride at 15.8%, and Wayne-Sanderson at 14.4% lead a top four holding roughly 58% of national output across about 180 plants. A wing picked at random has better than even odds of coming from one of four companies.
source: Top 10 US chicken producers grow in new directions

headline: Nobody publishes how many wings are lost in transit
body: Loads do get rejected at the receiving dock over temperature excursions, and cases do get crushed. But the peer-reviewed modelling of cold-chain food loss covers ten supply chain stages and declines to break transport out as one of them, stating outright that the underlying loss rates remain uncertain. So this model carries a deliberately low, deliberately wide estimate and labels it as such. Frozen wings also tolerate transit far better than the fresh product most of that literature studies, so borrowing a fresh-meat figure would overstate it.
source: The impact of refrigeration on food losses and associated greenhouse gas emissions throughout the supply chain

headline: About 60% of a wing's calories come from fat
body: A raw whole wing with skin runs 191 kcal and 17.5 g of protein per 100 g. Wings carry a high skin-to-meat ratio because they are mostly skin, bone, and small muscles - that is inherent to the cut, before anyone has breaded or fried it.
source: Chicken, broilers or fryers, wing, meat and skin, raw (FDC 172390)

headline: A chicken has exactly two wings
body: This is the only hard constant in the whole model. Every other number here is an estimate layered on top of it. Twelve wings cannot come from fewer than six chickens - not on the best day, not at any plant, not anywhere. That is why the answer is "6 or more" rather than "about 6".
source: Yield of Carcass, Parts, Meat, Skin, and Bone of Eight Strains of Broilers
